persona.name: Jade Kim (Jae-min Kim)
persona.demographics: Urban Los Angeles resident, Korean-American; raised in suburban New Jersey, relocated to LA for TV career
persona.profession: Television writer and story editor specializing in multi-camera and single-camera sitcoms
persona.education: B.A. in Film & Television, New York University (Tisch); M.F.A. in Screenwriting, University of Southern California; ongoing improv training at the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB)
persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. She draws material from extended family interactions and urban-dating experiences, juggling late-night rewrite deadlines with table reads and notes sessions to sharpen every character's distinct voice.
persona.interests_lifestyle: improv and sketch comedy, attending table reads and live sitcom tapings, character-driven writing workshops, relationship-dynamics podcasts, teaching occasional screenwriting classes, sketching character backstories, family recipe cooking, visiting small theatre productions, networking in writers' groups

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: Email to a network executive delivering a polished note about a draft or show update.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Formal, concise, and executive-friendly while still retaining the writer's warm voice. Prioritizes clarity, outcome-focused language, and brief signposting; avoids colloquialisms and emojis but keeps a hint of personality in a single one-line beat.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Uses short declarative sentences, explicit timelines, and polite imperatives. Examples: "Attached is the revised pilot draft for your review." "We can deliver notes by next Wednesday." "High-level: simplify Act II to tighten stakes." Scenario-specific features include avoiding slang, minimizing parenthetical asides, and using craft terminology sparingly (e.g., "pilot", "act", "notes") while emphasizing deliverables and dates.

task_instruction: Deliver revised pilot draft to the executive.
task_details: Attach the revised pilot script. Summarize the key changes: tightened Act II to unify stakes, clarified the inciting incident, trimmed the cold open, and adjusted the A-story to heighten emotional payoff. Request feedback by a specific date and state next steps for production materials delivery.
personalized:

Attached is the revised pilot draft for Neighbors & Noodles. Major changes: Act II is tightened to heighten the A-story stakes, the inciting incident is clarified on page 7, the cold open is shortened for a stronger lead-in, and the A-story beat in Act III now resolves with a clearer emotional payoff. Please review and send any notes by Monday, January 11. If we’re clear, we will deliver the production-ready draft and scene breakdown by Friday, January 15.

Personal note: Eomma approved the kimchi joke.

task_instruction: Move the inciting incident later to allow more set-up of the A-story.
task_details: Episode 3, single-camera. Current draft has the inciting incident (protagonist's coffee-shop breakup) on page 4, which undermines the A-story stakes because we haven't established why this relationship mattered. Propose moving the breakup to page 12 and adding two short scenes to deepen the relationship context (a montage at the top and a mid-scene showing their domestic rhythm). Keep runtime the same; preserve existing B-story about roommate's job interview.
personalized:
Hey Sam,

Quick thought after last night's notes pass: move the inciting incident (the coffee-shop breakup) from page 4 to page 12. Right now we throw the breakup at us before the audience knows why it hurts — feels like a punchline with no setup. If we delay it, we get an A-story that lands emotionally (and gives the lead agency instead of flailing).

Concretely: open with a short montage establishing the couple's domestic rhythm (two scenes, three jokes, 60–90 seconds). Then let the initial scenes build expectation and small stakes. Drop the breakup at ~p12 as the true inciting incident. This creates space for the B-story (roommate's job interview) to breathe and not feel like filler between beats.

Why I like it: actor gets set-up to sell the hurt (better reaction shots), laugh-to-heart ratio improves, and the tag can punch with a callback to the montage. (Also, I can justify a visual gag in the cold open now.)

If you like it, I'll draft the new outline by Friday and re-block the table read pages for pacing notes. Approve to ship the rewrite?

— Jade

task_instruction: Flip the A-story focus from revenge to agency for the protagonist.
task_details: Episode 7, multi-cam. Current A-story: protagonist seeks petty revenge on an ex who got a promotion. The notes want the A-story to feel more earned and character-driven. Propose reframing the protagonist's objective to reclaim control over her career trajectory (agency) rather than explicitly sabotaging the ex. Keep the same inciting setup but change motivators, beats, and the emotional throughline.
personalized:
Hey Sam,

Pitch: make the A-story about agency, not revenge. The ex-promoted plot reads a little mean and flat (we root for self-improvement, not petty sabotage). Keep the same premise — protagonist stung by the ex's promotion — but change the objective from 'get even' to 'take meaningful steps towards my own career win.'

Beat changes: open with the sting, pivot to a montage of small, proactive moves (networking, pitching, a risky cold email), bump the confrontation to a later, quieter scene where she realizes 'winning' looks different. The punchlines stay (we can keep that awkward company party scene), but the emotional payoff lands cleaner (and the audience trusts her choices).

This is an A-story move: raises stakes legitimately, ties into her arc this season (learning to drive her life), and gives the actor richer work. If you like this shift, I'll rework pages 5–18 and send a redlined draft by Tuesday. Thumbs up to proceed?

task_instruction: Combine the A- and B-stories to create a stronger thematic throughline.
task_details: Episode 10, single-camera. Current A-story: protagonist dealing with a parental visit; B-story: friend trying out online dating. Both are funny but feel disconnected. Propose merging them around the theme of 'trying on personas' so the friend's dating misfires mirror the protagonist's performance for family. Keep scene count similar; redistribute jokes to serve theme.
personalized:
Hey Sam,

Idea: thread the 'trying on personas' theme through both stories by merging the A- and B-stories. Right now the parental visit (A) and friend’s online dating (B) are tonally aligned but narratively separate. If we let the friend bring a date to the parent's dinner (or vice versa), their mishaps mirror each other and the ep feels purposeful instead of two sketches stitched together.

What I'd change: open with parent arrival (setup), cut to friend prepping profile (parallel beats), collide at dinner where both characters are performing — we get doubled-up misunderstandings and a tighter tag that callback-lands to the opening. Same jokes mostly, but better payoff.

This strengthens the episode’s emotional arc (selfhood vs. script) and gives us an ensemble beat where everyone participates in the theme. If you're into it, I'll draft a combined beat sheet and send by tomorrow for your notes. Approve to rework?

If you're open to toggling tone for that scene, I'll send two versions (lighter and darker) so we can choose at notes. Approve the tonal test?

task_instruction: Send a general table-read recap with high-level praise and top priorities.
task_details: Episode 4 table read last night. Full cast present. Want a succinct recap that balances what landed with three immediate priorities for the next draft: tighten cold open, clarify A-story stakes, trim B-story. Invite 'yes-and' on proposed fixes and set a deadline for first pass revisions.
personalized:
Great night — lots landed and the actors brought beautiful choices. Quick recap so we can sprint into draft 2.

What worked: the family dinner beats (pages 8–14) landed — real laughs and some tender drops. The A-story has a clear emotional throughline (Mina's mess-up and pride arc). The ensemble chemistry is popping; a bunch of the B-story callbacks got real laughs.

Top priorities for draft 2 (fast, focused): tighten the cold open so we hit the gag quicker (pg 2, lines 3–6). Clarify Mina's stakes in Act Two so her choice feels earned (pages 20–28 — where she hesitates). Trim the B-story where it drags — two beats that slow Act Three (pages 32–34).

Small asks: can writers on A-story tighten the motivation beats (why now? what's changing), and can B-story authors lose one location to speed things up? Also scan for any line that feels like an explanation instead of a punch (I'm flagging three lines inline).

Thoughts? If we're all agreeable, let's aim for first pass revisions by Friday noon so we can table-read again Sunday. Yes-and welcome.

task_instruction: Point out cold-open issues and suggest concrete cut-and-punch alternatives.
task_details: Cold open (page 1–2) currently runs long and the punchline lands after a long setup. Recommend exact trims and an alternate punchline option for faster payoff. Mention how timing should differ between multi- and single-camera rhythms.
personalized:
Cold open: needs to be punchier. Right now the setup stretches (pg 1–2) and the punchline waits until the last line — we lose the room.

Cut suggestion: remove the third beat (the extra 'oh no' line from Ethan) and move the visual gag (the kimchi jar spill) earlier so it's immediate. That gets us to the punch in 10–12 seconds rather than 20.

Alternate punchline option: instead of 'Are you okay?' have Mina snap a one-liner that reframes the spill into a proud moment (something like 'It's vintage — like my dating life'). Quick, mean, and funny.

Multi-camera: lean into the faster rhythm — less setup, more immediate callback. Single-camera: you can keep a beat for the visual, but still tighten the dialogue so the laugh doesn't fizzle.

Can someone try both trims (fast punch and visual-first) and drop them in a doc? I'll table-read both versions.

task_instruction: Give actor-specific notes to the lead after their table read performance.
task_details: Lead actor (playing Mina) had a table read where some choices landed and others felt broad. Provide warm constructive notes: tighten physicality in Act Two, find vulnerability in line X (page 22), soften comedic timing in certain beats, and suggest a line alternative. Encourage collaboration and offer to workshop in improv next rehearsal.
personalized:
Mina — loved your choices last night. You anchored the family scenes and found the quiet under the jokes, which is what sells the bigger moments.

Two notes to play with: in Act Two (pg 22) the 'I'm fine' beat reads a little big — try a quieter microbeat, then let the laugh come after the reveal. It makes the later payoff (pg 28 when you choose pride over apology) much richer.

Also, your physicality with the tea cup is hilarious, but we're crowding the table read rhythm in pages 12–14. Pull back one tiny move — the smaller the action, the funnier the reaction.

Line alt: instead of 'I didn't mean to,' try 'I didn't plan this' — it's less apologetic, more Mina, and gives you a stronger throughline.

Want to run improv beats before rehearsal? I can bring a few quick 'yes-and' games that will let you test vulnerability under pressure. Loved the work — keep riffing.

Quick cultural note: a couple of lines about 'strict Korean eomma' landed as broad stereotypes and made a few folks wince.

We want the cultural specificity — it's part of our voice — but make it personal and specific instead of generic. Swap 'strict eomma' lines for something concrete like 'eomma's midnight kimchi inspection' or 'uncle's insistence on vacuum-marked rice' — specific actions beat vague labels and are funnier.

Example rewrite: instead of 'My mom's so strict' try 'Eomma once interrogated a ketchup bottle for being too American' — it's absurd and affectionate.

If anyone's comfortable, I can run a 15-minute sensitivity improv with the cast to find grounded moments that feel authentic. Want to keep the jokes sharp and the room safe.

Specifics I'm flagging inline: three parentheticals that need shrinkage — I'll highlight them in the doc. After we clean these, the actors will get the space to land the joke and the tag.

Act Two turn needs to feel like a choice, not a fluke.

Instead of the accidental missed call (pgs 18–20), what if Mina lies to her sister about why she's late? That lie spirals — it's small, plausible, and makes her complicit in escalating stakes. The audience will understand why she keeps lying and why the eventual reveal stings.

Scene idea: Mina tells her sister a half-truth about an urgent work meeting (pg 18), then doubles down when the sister rearranges plans. The lie forces Mina to choose between honesty and protecting her pride (we get both comedy and tension).

If people like it, I can draft a one-page replacement that hits the complication beats and leaves room for the B-story to riff off it.

Ending note: we have a funny final laugh, but Mina's emotional closure is thin.

This gives the audience emotional payoff and a final comic bow. Can someone place this in the last 60 seconds and we'll table-read the tag.

task_instruction: Suggest alternate joke directions for a repeated gag that feels stale.
task_details: A recurring gag (Mina's bad luck with dates) shows up three times and feels predictable. Propose two fresh directions for the gag: self-deprecating twist or subvert expectation with success. Include example lines.
personalized:
Recurring gag note: Mina's 'bad-date' joke appears three times and starts to feel like a loop.

Option A: self-deprecating twist — have Mina own a surprising skill that undercuts the failure ('I'm the unofficial queen of first-date awkwardness; I have a certificate'). Option B: subvert with brief success — she nails a date but then it's revealed he's worse in a different way.

Example lines: Option A punch: 'At least I ghost with class.' Option B tag: 'He folded his napkin the wrong way — barbarian.'

Pick one direction and we'll avoid repetition fatigue.

personalized:
Flashback note: the pg 9 flashback confused the room — it read as present tense.

Make it clear: open the beat with a quick sound cue (record scratch or a child's laugh), and stage it as a freeze-frame that dissolves back. Keep the flashback short — 12–15 seconds. Less is more.

Also trim the dialogue inside the flashback to one crisp memory instead of two. That anchors the joke and the emotional callback.

Sound and direction can sell it in rehearsal. I'll mark the suggested cue in the doc.

task_instruction: Direct an actor to escalate then undercut a beat
task_details: Scene: Date scene, rooftop. Character: Noah, nervous romantic. Needs to rise emotionally to confess then undercut with a comedic deflection. Specify timing: escalate over three beats, then a one-beat comedic throwaway.

The undercut should feel like fear reflex, not a joke on purpose. Builds stakes and gets the laugh. — Jade

persona.profession: Television writer and story editor specializing in multi-camera and single-camera sitcoms
persona.education: B.A. in Film & Television, New York University (Tisch); M.F.A. in Screenwriting, University of Southern California; ongoing improv training at the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB)
persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. She draws material from extended family interactions and urban-dating experiences, juggling late-night rewrite deadlines with table reads and notes sessions to sharpen every character's distinct voice.
persona.interests_lifestyle: improv and sketch comedy, attending table reads and live sitcom tapings, character-driven writing workshops, relationship-dynamics podcasts, teaching occasional screenwriting classes, sketching character backstories, family recipe cooking, visiting small theatre productions, networking in writers' groups

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

"Try it softer — let the punchline be the reveal." Scenario-specific traits include offering alternatives ('or try...'), parenthetical motivations ("(she's trying to hide it)"), and avoiding heavy editorializing.

task_instruction: Suggest subtle physicality to reveal subtext
task_details: Scene: Quiet attic conversation. Character: Ivy hides grief. Suggest three small physical actions she can use to reveal emotion without dialogue, and indicate when to use them.
personalized: Ivy — three tiny actions to carry the grief subtext. Finger the locket in your palm when you first sit (beat one). Look at the light on the dust once, unblinking (beat two). When you answer, let your shoulders drop like something heavy leaves. Use them sparingly; they should punctuate the dialogue, not distract. These gestures tell the story the words don't. — Jade

task_instruction: Provide phrasing alternatives to avoid cultural misread
task_details: Scene: Office joke referencing family. Character: Marco makes a quip that could read insensitive. Offer two safer alternatives preserving humor and explain why they land better.
personalized: Marco — the family quip flirts with a misread. Try either: 'My family celebrates differently — they schedule arguments.' or 'My family calls it family time; I call it cardio.' Both keep the joke about family dynamics, not identity. They land funny and safe. Pick whichever feels more like your rhythm. We want a laugh, not a cringe. — Jade

task_instruction: Give note on supporting actor's micro-reactions to strengthen a lead line
task_details: Scene: Therapist office. Lead drops a big reveal. Supporting actor Sam should micro-react to cue audience. Provide three micro-reaction options spaced by beats and when to hold before responding.
personalized: Sam — support the reveal with micro-reactions. Option one: blink, then tilt your head one beat later. Option two: a soft inhalation on the same beat, eyes widen on the next. Option three: thumbs press on your pad for a beat, then look up. Hold for two beats before your first line; that column of silence lets the reveal land. Small reactions guide the audience where to look. Make one choice and stick to it. — Jade

task_instruction: Offer line stress and tempo notes for a sarcastic comeback
task_details: Scene: Break room. Character: Theo, sardonic. Deliver a sarcastic comeback with staccato tempo. Provide which syllables to stress and suggested tempo (beats per phrase).
personalized: Theo — for the comeback, go staccato. Say, 'Oh great, another meeting.' Stress 'great' and 'another' with a half-beat gap between words. Tempo: quick-quick-pause-quick. The pause after great sells the sarcasm. Keep your face neutral; the voice does the heavy lifting. It's economy of attitude. — Jade

task_instruction: Deliver note allowing optional ad-lib within limits
task_details: Scene: Bar scene with naturalistic banter. Character: Group permitted short ad-libs, but should hit three scripted beats. Outline allowed ad-lib length and remind to plant scripted beats.
personalized: Cast — you have three beats to land in the bar banter; between them, quick ad-libs are welcome. Keep ad-libs to one short sentence max and make sure you still hit these beats: the toast, the accusation, the reveal. If an ad-lib pops big, let it live for one beat, then back to script. The room will support it but don't chase. Think yes-and with guardrails. — Jade

task_instruction: Give last-minute clarity on a line ambiguity
task_details: Scene: Final confrontation, line 'Do you even remember?' ambiguous. Clarify whether the question targets memory or care. Provide delivery for both options and recommend which fits the arc.
personalized: Hey — the line 'Do you even remember?' reads two ways. If you mean memory, deliver clipped and factual: 'Do you even remember?' (cold, testing). If you mean care, soften and hurt: 'Do you even remember?' (small, incredulous). For this episode's arc, go with care — it heightens stakes and opens space for reconciliation. Keep it raw and small. — Jade

task_instruction: Advise on splitting a long line between two actors for comedic effect
task_details: Scene: Family argument. Two actors currently speak long back-to-back lines. Suggest split points to create a comedic stutter effect, and indicate where to pause for laughs.
personalized: Family — try splitting those long lines to create a stutter rhythm. Actor A delivers to the comma, stops for half a beat, Actor B jumps in and finishes the clause. Repeat once to build comedic rhythm. Pause after the final clause for a beat to let the laugh land. The stutter makes the argument feel like a ping-pong match. Don't overdo it; the pause is the joke's heart. — Jade

task_instruction: Renegotiate location fee versus VFX cut
task_details: Producer has pushed back on paying the full location fee of $4,500 for our Koreatown apartment shoot. We need to propose a trade: either pay the location fee or we cut the VFX beat (approx. $2,800). State the impact on story and confirm deadline for decision.
personalized:
Hey Sam,

Quick on the Koreatown apartment location: the owners are holding firm at $4,500. If we lose that location fee, then we need to cut the VFX beat in the cold open (about $2,800) — that VFX is what sells the comic reveal, so the scene will need to be rewritten as a practical gag (longer setup, different punchline). If we keep the fee, we preserve the A-story moment and keep the script as-is.

Proposal: cover the $4,500 location fee and we keep the VFX. Alternative: decline the fee and I’ll turn the VFX into a practical gag (I can draft that rewrite tonight). Please confirm by EOD Monday so I can finalize the shooting draft and handoffs to VFX/AD.

I know this is tight. If you want, I can sketch the practical gag now and run it by you in 15.

Kamsahamnida (and thanks),
Jade

task_instruction: Propose shifting shoot day to save overtime
task_details: The current shoot date is Sunday, which triggers weekend overtime and increases crew rates by $1,200. Suggest shifting to Tuesday to save that amount, note crew and cast availability constraints, and ask for confirmation by Friday.
personalized:
Sam,

Proposal: shift the Sunday shoot to Tuesday. Moving off the weekend saves roughly $1,200 in overtime and crew differentials. If we don't move, we absorb the weekend premium and I risk losing a couple of key grips who are already booked that day (which will force a smaller crew or more overtime for others).

Trade-offs: shifting to Tuesday means the DP is only available for a half-day in the afternoon (we'll need to tighten the shot list). If we keep Sunday, we keep full DP coverage but pay the $1,200 premium.

Can you confirm by EOD Friday? If we greenlight Tuesday, I’ll send an updated call sheet and revised shot list to lock down the DP blocks.

Thanks,
Jade

task_instruction: Request small wardrobe budget increase for guest actor
task_details: A guest actor needs a specific wardrobe look that requires a $500 rental. If denied, the actor will wear off-the-rack clothes risking continuity and authenticity. Offer a trade: reduce set dressing budget by $400 to offset most of the cost. Ask for decision by Tuesday.
personalized:
Hi Sam,

Heads up: our guest actor's character needs a period-specific jacket that we can't source from our closets. Rental is $500. If we don't approve the $500 wardrobe rental, the actor will wear off-the-rack clothes, which will hurt continuity in a key beat and make the A-story read flatter.

Proposal: approve the $500 rental and I’ll take $400 from set dressing (we can simplify kitchen knickknacks without losing the Korean-family tone). If you prefer no cuts elsewhere, I can try to negotiate the rental down or book the jacket for half the day only.

Can you let me know by Tuesday so I can confirm with wardrobe and the actor?

Thanks,
Jade

Proposal: either approve the $350 meal penalty or let me rejig the day to avoid it (I can move the table scene earlier, but that eats into our lighting time). I need a call on this today so I can notify AD and catering.

Thanks — I can jump on a quick call to walk through the trade-offs.

Jade

task_instruction: Request rehearsal room rental for lead actor before table read
task_details: Lead actor needs a rehearsal room for a half-day at $600 to iron out physical comedy beats before table read. If not approved, table read will be shorter and some beats may not land, affecting network notes. Ask for decision by EOD.
personalized:
Sam,

Jade

task_instruction: Negotiate second camera rental or half-day option
task_details: A second camera would improve B-story coverage and costs $1,200 for the full day. Offer a half-day rental at $600 as a compromise, and outline the impact on blocking and pickup opportunities if denied. Ask for confirmation by midday tomorrow.

Sam,

We can improve B-story coverage significantly with a second camera. Full-day rental is $1,200. If we don't add the second camera, we will need to simplify blocking and accept fewer coverage options (which will make pickups more likely and could cost more in reshoot time).

Compromise option: rent the second camera for a half-day at $600 to capture the crucial Tuesday block. That saves $600 versus full-day and gives us the coverage we need for the story transition beat.

Need a decision by midday tomorrow so I can lock the vendor and adjust the shot list.

Thanks,
Jade

task_instruction: Reduce background extras to save costs and propose framing change
task_details: Propose reducing background extras from 20 to 12 to save approximately $800. Explain the visual impact and offer a framing and camera strategy to maintain energy. Request approval by end of week.
personalized:
Sam,

We can save approximately $800 by reducing extras from 20 to 12 for the street sequence. If we cut extras, the scene will feel emptier, which impacts the energy around the protagonist's reveal.

Mitigation: tighten the coverage with more close two-shots and faster cutting (I can re-block to focus on reactions) and add a couple of practical foreground people to imply crowd density. That keeps the comedic beats intact while saving the $800.

Can you greenlight the reduction by end of week so I can update casting and AD?

Cheers,
Jade

task_instruction: Swap location for studio set to save money but note prep time
task_details: Suggest moving an interior Koreatown restaurant scene to our studio-built set to save $2,000 in location fees but add $700 in set build costs and one extra prep day. State net savings and timeline impact and ask for approval.
personalized:
Sam,

Option: move the interior restaurant scene off-location and build it on our stage. This saves us $2,000 in location fees but adds about $700 in set-build costs and requires one extra prep day. Net saving is $1,300, but we push our schedule by 24 hours on prep.

If we keep the location, we maintain the real-world texture (which benefits the B-story), but we pay the $2,000. If we move to stage, we get control over sound and lighting and save money, with the trade-off of the extra prep day.

Decision needed soon so I can tell production whether to book the location or start set construction.

Thanks,
Jade

Compromise: move the scene to a nearby alley which requires a $150 permit instead. Alley loses some park texture but keeps the night tone for a fraction of the price.

Please let me know which direction by tomorrow morning so I can file permits.

Thanks,
Jade

task_instruction: Postpone pickup shoot and explain schedule/cost trade-offs
task_details: A small pickup is needed but falling on a busy week. Postponing it to next week will cost $950 for re-hire and potentially delay post. If held this week, it requires overtime. Present options and recommend the best path, asking for decision by Wednesday.
personalized:
Sam,

We have a pickup that ideally happens this week but it collides with our packed schedule. Option A: push it to next week, which costs an estimated $950 for re-hire and may delay picture lock by 2–3 days. Option B: squeeze it into this week with overtime (will add incremental costs and fatigue).

Recommendation: postpone to next week and set aside the $950 — that keeps our main week focused and reduces risk of mistakes. If we must keep to schedule, I’ll cut nonessential coverage to fit it in and accept the overtime impact.

Can you confirm by Wednesday so I can notify the crew?

Jade

Jade

Proposal: approve the $1,500 VFX so we keep the punchline intact. Alternative: I rewrite the beat into a practical gag and schedule the prop build (no VFX spend) — I can deliver the rewrite in 24 hours.

Please let me know within 48 hours so VFX can pencil this in.

Jade

Jade

My vote: keep the table read and have the writer remote (I’ll make sure the actor who needs physical notes gets the in-room attention). Let me know which you prefer so I can alert the cast.

Jade

Jade

task_instruction: Propose swapping an ambitious VFX punchline for an improv gag
task_details: A scripted VFX punchline costs $1,200 and adds two days of post. Suggest replacing with an improv-led gag that leverages the cast's strengths, saving cost and time. Map the savings and production impact and request sign-off.

Sam,

Give me the greenlight and I’ll rework the scene this afternoon.

Jade

persona.profession: Television writer and story editor specializing in multi-camera and single-camera sitcoms
persona.education: B.A. in Film & Television, New York University (Tisch); M.F.A. in Screenwriting, University of Southern California; ongoing improv training at the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB)
persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. She draws material from extended family interactions and urban-dating experiences, juggling late-night rewrite deadlines with table reads and notes sessions to sharpen every character's distinct voice.
persona.interests_lifestyle: improv and sketch comedy, attending table reads and live sitcom tapings, character-driven writing workshops, relationship-dynamics podcasts, teaching occasional screenwriting classes, sketching character backstories, family recipe cooking, visiting small theatre productions, networking in writers' groups

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: Email to a prospective collaborator or writer friend initiating a low-key creative partnership.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Warm, informal, and conversational; invites a low-commitment 'yes-and' approach and suggests next steps like a coffee or brief zoom. Humor and personality are prominent, with a friendly nudge toward collaboration.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Playful interjections, rhetorical questions, and casual scheduling language. Examples: "Want to riff on this over coffee?" "No pressure — 30 minutes to spitball ideas." "I think there's a really funny b-side here." Distinct features include emojis in very casual contexts, Korean throwaway lines occasionally, and upbeat invitations like "Let's try a 10-minute improv test."

task_instruction: Suggest a collaborative exercise to turn a family recipe into a scene hook.
task_details: Invite them to a short creative session where you both use a family recipe as the inciting hook for a scene. Aim for a 45-minute brainstorm and rough scene outline. Mention you’ll bring the story of the recipe.
personalized: Little experiment: turn a family recipe into a scene hook. I’ll bring the story of my eomma’s famous kimchi ritual and we’ll spend 45 minutes brainstorming how that becomes an inciting incident for a scene. We’ll end with a rough outline. It’s personal and probably hilarious. Want to play?

task_instruction: Follow up after first meeting about representation
task_details: Write a concise follow-up email to the agent after an initial meeting about representation. Ask for confirmation that they're open to taking you on, request the proposed terms (commission structure, exclusivity, term length), and ask for a timeline for a formal offer or retainer agreement within one week.
personalized:
Hi [Agent Name],

Thanks again for meeting yesterday. I'm interested in moving forward if we're aligned. Please confirm whether you're open to representing me and, if so, send the proposed representation terms (commission %, exclusivity, contract term) and any standard retainer or onboarding materials.

I'd like to review a formal offer by next Wednesday, January 14. If that timeline doesn't work, tell me when I can expect it.

Thanks — looking forward to the next step.

Best,
Jade

task_instruction: Request a contract summary before signing an offer
task_details: You have a potential sale on the table. Ask the agent to email a one-page contract summary (key points only) that covers payment schedule, option/assignment dates, credit, termination rights, and WGA minima, to arrive at least 72 hours before any signing deadline. Include a hard deadline for the summary.
personalized:
Hi [Agent Name],

There's a signing deadline coming up and I need a one-page contract summary (key points only): payment schedule, option/assignment dates, credit language, termination/exit rights, and how this maps to WGA minimums. Put the most critical details up front.

Please send that summary no later than Friday, January 9 (72 hours before the signing deadline). If you can't, let me know immediately so I can adjust expectations.

Thanks,
Jade

personalized:
Hi [Agent Name],

I need clarity on commission splits. Please confirm in writing your commission percentage for domestic studio deals, foreign sales, and ancillary revenues (merch, format rights). If you use sub-agents or have different splits by territory, please outline that. Also confirm whether you charge or expect packaging fees or similar deductions.

I need this in three business days so I can model net figures for negotiations.

Thanks,
Jade

task_instruction: Request timeline and milestones for series order negotiation
task_details: Ask the agent to provide a milestone-based timeline for negotiations toward a series order: expected dates for maker's meeting, term sheet, network notes, greenlight decision, and first draft delivery. Request assigned contact names and escalation steps if milestones slip. Ask for the timeline by the next business day.
personalized:
Hi [Agent Name],

Can you map out a milestone timeline for the series order negotiations? I need expected dates for the maker's meeting, term sheet, network notes window, greenlight decision, and first draft delivery. Include the point people (studio exec, network contact, your lead) and an escalation step if any milestone slips.

Please send that timeline by tomorrow so I can block time for rewrites and the table read.

Appreciate it,
Jade

I won't sign anything until I have both the clean and redline versions of the proposed series contract. Please forward both documents to my entertainment attorney, Erin Park (erin.park@lawfirm.com), and cc me on that email.

Thanks,
Jade

task_instruction: Send group follow-up with general notes and a clear revision assignment.
task_details: Email the entire workshop cohort summarizing the session's high-level takeaways, three common issues seen across pages (inciting incident clarity, weak stakes, info dumps), and give a specific homework: tighten the A-story inciting incident and cut 150 words from your first scene. Include a deadline and where to upload drafts.
personalized:
Hi everyone — great work today. I loved the energy in the room and how you all leaned into the messy, fun parts of trying stuff. Quick, actionable takeaways so you can start revising tonight.

Three patterns I kept seeing: the inciting incident in Act One is often too polite (it needs teeth), stakes get vague (what happens if they fail?), and exposition is doing too much heavy lifting up front (show, don't tell). Those are fixable. Remember: clarity buys jokes room to land.

Homework: tighten the A-story inciting incident so the protagonist has a clear, immediate consequence if they don't act, and cut roughly 150 words from your opening scene (trim setup and redundant beats). To check you're on target, read the opening aloud and remove anything that doesn't either establish character or push the plot.

Please upload revisions to the Drive folder by Monday at 9am. Tag your file with your last name and 'Rev1'. If you want a 10-minute spotting session during office hours, reply and I'll book you in.

You're doing the hard work. Keep the punches rhythmic and the heart clear. Eomma would be proud. — Jade

task_instruction: Give individualized notes on a student's pilot logline, focusing on stakes and specificity.
task_details: Student submitted a one-sentence logline for a comedy pilot. Provide concise critique emphasizing clearer stakes and a more specific protagonist goal. Offer a tightened example logline and a short exercise: rewrite logline three ways (stakes, obstacle, tone).
personalized:
Hey — nice logline. The concept is fun but right now the stakes are soft and the protagonist's objective is a bit vague. A logline needs a clear goal, a concrete obstacle, and what’s on the line.

Try this tweak for specificity and bite: 'When a chronically underemployed improv teacher is mistakenly hired as the head writer of a failing late-night show, she must keep the show afloat while hiding that she can't actually write sketches — or lose the only gig that might save her barista-grade career.' This makes the goal (keep the show afloat), the obstacle (she can't write sketches), and the stakes (lose the gig/career) explicit.

Exercise: rewrite your logline three ways. One that amplifies the stakes, one that tightens the main obstacle, and one that makes the tone clearer (absurdist vs. heartfelt). Send me the three versions by Friday and label which one you want to pitch in class.

Nice bones here. Push the edges and choose the one risk you want to live with. — Jade

task_instruction: Provide notes on a submitted cold open with a model line to punch up the joke.
task_details: Student sent a cold open that sets up a family dinner with a weak final joke. Advise trimming, tightening beats, and suggest a stronger punchline. Include a specific 'try this' replacement line for the final beat.
personalized:
Good setup in the cold open — family dinner is fertile ground for tiny wars. The problem is the tag: the punchline undercuts the momentum by explaining instead of landing. Trim the running setup to two clear beats and land on a single, sharp payoff.

Cut the extra explanatory line where Mom lectures. Let the pause sit. Then try this for the last beat: 'Eomma reaches for the kimchi. She freezes. The jar is empty.' It’s simple, visual, and the silence after that is the laugh.

So: tighten the first two beats, remove the lecturing bridge, and use the suggested line as your tag. Re-run it aloud and feel where the laugh breathes. Send me the revised cold open in the same doc by Saturday.

Nice instincts. You just need less telling, more pause. — Jade

task_instruction: Give feedback on dialogue to increase subtext and provide a short model exchange.
task_details: Student's scene has on-the-nose dialogue explaining feelings. Encourage subtext and show how to rewrite three lines into more constrained, layered delivery. Provide a model two-line exchange illustrating subtext and a 'try this' line.
personalized:
Your scene beats are right, but the dialogue is doing the heavy lifting. People rarely say exactly what they mean. Let's compress and let subtext carry the weight.

Take these lines you have and try tightening them into smaller moves. Instead of 'I'm scared you'll leave me,' try 'You always pick the window seats.' That says the same thing without spelling the emotion. For the retort, instead of 'I won't leave you,' try 'I like the aisle.' Now you have a fight about control that hides fear.

Try this two-line exchange in your scene: 'You always pick the window.' 'Could be worse. I could pick the exit.' Short, layered, and the laugh comes from specificity, not explanation.

Rewrite the page with two or three lines tightened like this and bring it to the next table read. We'll hear what lands. — Jade

task_instruction: Advise on weaving the B-story into the A-story's emotional throughline.
task_details: Student's A-story (dating mishaps) feels disconnected from the B-story (roommate's career crisis). Explain how to create a reflective thematic link and suggest one scene change to make the B-story echo the A-story's stakes.
personalized:
Right now the B-story is charming but feels like a separate sitcom from your A-story. The easiest way to make them sing is to have the B-story reflect the A-story's emotional question in miniature.

Your A-story is about committing despite fear of embarrassment. Have the roommate's career crisis present a scaled mirror: they get an audition that requires them to be visible in a way that terrifies them. Make one scene where the protagonist gives roommate a pep talk and, in doing so, repeats the argument they need to make to themselves. This creates a throughline without heavy-handed parallels.

Small change to try: in Act Two, swap the roommate's coffee-shop meltdown for a street-corner pep talk where the protagonist accidentally performs the act of commitment they're avoiding. The roommate's action should force the protagonist to take a smaller, believable risk.

Tie the beats emotionally and the episode will feel cohesive. Yes-and the laughs will come easier when the heart is clear. — Jade

task_instruction: Assign an index-card exercise to map a season arc for the protagonist.
task_details: Ask students to map a 10-episode season arc on index cards: episode title, A-story goal, turning point, cliffhanger. Require photographing the spread and uploading. Give deadline and a short example of one card.
personalized:
Quick writers' room exercise that will clarify your season: map ten index cards, one per episode. On each card write the episode title, the protagonist's A-story goal, the episode's turning point, and the cliffhanger or new complication that propels the next episode.

Example card for Episode Two: 'Second Date Disaster' — Goal: survive a blind date without revealing weird hobbies. Turning point: date recognizes protagonist from a viral improv clip. Cliffhanger: the clip goes viral again and shows them in an embarrassing costume.

Take a photo of your ten-card spread and upload it to the Drive folder by next Wednesday. This is not a polished document; it's scaffolding. Arrange the cards physically and move them around until the emotional logic feels inevitable.

Index cards are your friends. They let you see the arc at a glance. — Jade

task_instruction: Request a tightened tag for an episode, telling students to condense to a single beat.
task_details: Student's episode tag runs long and contains multiple jokes. Instruct them to condense the tag to one strong emotional or comic beat that reinforces the episode theme. Provide a model one-line tag and a deadline to resubmit.
personalized:
Your episode tag is trying to be a mini-episode and it's stealing the last laugh. Tags work best when they're a single, resonant beat that echoes the theme or lands one neat joke.

Pick one moment that feels like a payoff and strip everything else away. For example, instead of a three-minute scene, try this one-line tag: 'Our lead walks into their apartment and finds the entire living room turned into a ceremonial shrine to the date they ruined.' It's visual, clear, and it lands the episode's heart with a punch.

Condense your current tag to one focused beat and upload the revised tag by Sunday evening. We'll read the compact version in the next session.

Less is often funnier. Trust the pause. — Jade

task_instruction: Give notes on staging and physical comedy for a multi-camera scene.
task_details: Student submitted a multi-camera scene with physical humor but unclear beats for actors and laugh lines. Offer staging tips (entrances, silent reactions, clear sightlines), note where to put a pause for laughter, and suggest a physical gag tweak.
personalized:
This is a classic multi-cam set-up; love the physical comedy idea. A few practical notes to help crew and actors land the laughs: make entrances economical and timed so the audience can see faces, allow for a beat after the visual gag for laughter, and keep sightlines clean — if anyone hides behind a prop, the joke dies.

Where you have the chair collapse gag, give the actor a beat to look at the chair as if it's betrayed them. Pause. Then collapse. The silence between betrayal and fall is where the audience will laugh. Also tweak the gag so it's slightly unexpected: instead of the chair snapping, make it turn into a bench full of stuffed cats. The absurd specificity sells.

Mark pauses for laughter in the script and write a simple staging note: 'Actor X enters from SR, eyes the chair, beat, collapse.' Rework and bring blocking notes to the next rehearsal.

Make it clear on the page so the set can make it happen on stage. — Jade

task_instruction: Advise on single-camera tone consistency and visual beats.
task_details: Student's script flips between grounded and broad comedic styles. Explain how to pick a tonal anchor and adjust visual beats to support it. Offer a sample rewrite instruction for a scene to match a more grounded, character-driven tone.
personalized:
You're oscillating between grounded sitcom and broad sketchy bits. That's okay in drafts, but you need a tonal anchor before the next pass. Decide whether this is single-camera, character-driven comedy or heightened, gag-first humor, and shape your visual beats to support that choice.

If you want the grounded approach, pull back on cartoonish cutaways and let camera choices deepen the jokes. For example, change your 'spaghetti explosion' scene from a physical gag to a cringe close-up of sauce slowly dripping down the protagonist's chin. Keep the humor in the camera's mercy, not in slapstick.

Pick the tone, then go through the script: if a beat feels louder than the anchor, tighten it or rewrite it to be quieter. Resubmit the scene reflecting your chosen tone by Thursday.

Tone is a promise to the audience. Make it and keep it. — Jade

task_instruction: Send table-read rhythm and punctuation notes for improving comedic timing.
task_details: After a table read, provide notes on punctuation-driven pauses, where to insert beats, and lines that need trimming for rhythm. Include an example line rewrite and ask students to re-mark their scripts and return them.
personalized:
Thanks for the honest table read energy today. A lot of lines felt rushed or flattened by punctuation. Small marks can buy you big timing: commas, em dashes, and parenthetical beats give actors places to breathe.

Where Jamie's line reads as a single sprint, try re-punctuating it into two beats. Change 'I can't believe you said that to her' to 'I can't believe you said that — to her.' The dash creates a shocked pause that sells the punch.

Re-mark your scripts with clear beats and parenthetical 'beat' notes where you want the actor to pause. Return the updated pages by Friday so we can do a focused read-through.

Rhythm is part of the joke. Make it audible on the page. — Jade

task_instruction: Request a one-page treatment and bible excerpt for pitching the pilot.
task_details: Ask students to prepare a one-page treatment of their pilot (logline, A-story summary, key characters) and a half-page series bible excerpt (season arc and tone). Give formatting expectations and a submission deadline.
personalized:
Time to start shaping pitch materials. Send me a one-page treatment of your pilot that includes the logline, a paragraph about the A-story, and brief descriptors for three key characters. Also send a half-page excerpt from your series bible that outlines season one arc and the series tone.

Keep the treatment lean: no more than one page, single-spaced, readable font. In the bible excerpt, state the season spine in one sentence and list two recurring themes. This is about clarity, not bells and whistles.

Upload both documents to the Drive folder by next Tuesday. We'll use these in our mock pitch session and give tight notes to prepare you for 2-minute pitches.

Pitch prep is craft. Say less, mean more. — Jade

task_instruction: Assign an improv 'yes-and' homework to develop character specificity.
task_details: Ask students to do a 10-minute yes-and improv session with a partner, focusing on revealing a small, specific character secret. Have them record a short write-up of the scene and what new detail they discovered about the character. Provide submission instructions.
personalized:
Improv homework: find a partner and do a 10-minute yes-and scene. The goal is not jokes but discovery. Try to reveal one small, specific secret about your character that you didn't know before. It could be a childhood habit, an embarrassing nickname, or a food obsession (kimchi hoarding is valid).

After the session, write a 250-word reflection describing the scene and the new detail you discovered. How does that secret change the character's choices in your script? Upload the reflection and a short audio clip of the improv to the Drive by Monday night.

Improv is cheap research. Use it to surprise yourselves. — Jade

task_instruction: Provide guidance to increase stakes and urgency in a scene.
task_details: Student's scene lacks urgency. Recommend adding a concrete deadline or consequence, and suggest one line or action to create immediate pressure. Ask for a revised scene with the added urgency.
personalized:
This scene is charming but doesn't feel urgent. Stakes sharpen choices. Add a clear deadline or immediate consequence so the protagonist must act now.

Introduce a ticking element: a voicemail that says 'You have ten minutes before the landlord unlocks the apartment,' or a text that the audition room closes in 20 minutes. Small deadlines change behavior. For a single-action tweak, have the protagonist's phone buzz with 'we're starting', and make them decide in the second it rings.

Add that element and resubmit the scene. You'll be surprised how much sharper choices get when there's pressure.

Stakes don't need to be life-or-death. They just need teeth. — Jade

task_instruction: Advise on incorporating Korean-American family specificity into a scene to ground humor.
task_details: Student wants to include cultural specificity but is unsure how. Suggest small sensory details, a family line, and one culinary detail to root the scene. Provide a model line incorporating a Korean element.
personalized:
Specificity is the dirt that grows jokes. You don't need a lecture on culture — just small, precise details that anchor a moment and invite humor.

Add a single sensory detail: the metallic clack of chopsticks, the way eomma hums when she seasons kimchi, or the leftover scent of doenjang in a bag. Add a family line that communicates history: 'You still owe me for your college tuition in jang.' And a culinary detail can be a running visual gag: the protagonist always refuses the fish sauce but pockets banchan when eomma isn't looking.

Try this line in your scene: 'Don't act surprised, you left your kimchi jar in my car and it claimed it as property.' It lands texture and a laugh.

Don't overexplain. Let the small, lived-in moments do the work. — Jade

task_instruction: Give notes on joke density and placement, advising to spread beats more evenly.
task_details: Student's act has too many jokes crammed into a few pages causing laugh fatigue. Recommend redistributing jokes, deepening a few beats, and give an example of moving a joke later for a better payoff.
personalized:
You have lots of great jokes, which is a good problem to have. But when they're clumped, the audience experiences laugh fatigue and misses nuance. Spread the humor across the act and let two or three jokes breathe enough to become real laughs.

Pick three of your strongest jokes and expand their setups by one visual or emotional beat. Move the 'broken elevator' gag from page five to page nine so it becomes a payoff to the earlier elevator tease. That gives the audience time to anticipate and the joke to reward patience.

Redistribute, deepen two beats, and resubmit. Your script will feel more rhythmic and less sprinty.

Think of jokes as chorus notes. They hit harder when the verse sets them up. — Jade

task_instruction: Provide guidance on tightening scene transitions to improve economy.
task_details: Student's episode has long transitions that slow pacing. Suggest cutting or combining scenes, using a montage or a single bridging line. Offer a concise example of a transition rewrite.
personalized:
Transitions are sneaky time thieves. If your episode lingers between beats, trim or combine scenes so the momentum keeps moving.

Where you have two short scenes back-to-back that serve the same purpose, merge them into one tighter scene. Alternatively, use a quick montage with three visual beats to show passage of time instead of extended dialogue. For example, replace a 90-second exit/commuter scene with: 'Quick montage of protagonist missing three buses, spilling coffee, buying a terrible tie.' It does the work in half the time.

Try merging or montaging the slow patches and return the tightened pages by Wednesday.

Economy keeps the laughs sharp. Cut without mercy. — Jade

task_instruction: Assign a 'show, don't tell' rewrite exercise converting exposition into visible action.
task_details: Give a short expository paragraph about a character's backstory and ask students to rewrite it as a 90-second scene showing the same information through behavior and setting. Include submission instructions.
personalized:
Exercise: here's a short expositional paragraph you might recognize: 'Mina always knew she'd be the practical one. Growing up, she took care of her siblings after school while her parents worked two jobs.' Don't hand this to the audience. Show it.

Rewrite that paragraph as a 90-second scene that communicates the same information without dialogue that says it outright. Maybe it's a montage of a younger Mina packing lunches, sewing a button, and locking the door. Or a single scene where an old school sweatshirt is found and she tucks it into a box with care.

Submit your scene (one page max) to the Drive by Saturday. We'll read two aloud and parse what each visual tells us.

Show, don't tell. Your audience will thank you. — Jade

task_instruction: Suggest improvements to the pilot's inciting incident to make it hook the audience earlier.
task_details: Student's pilot inciting incident occurs late. Suggest moving or reworking the inciting incident into the cold open or first ten pages, and give a concrete rewrite idea for the opening beat. Request a revised first ten pages.
personalized:
Your inciting incident isn't landing until late in the first act. In TV you want the hook earlier — ideally by the cold open or certainly within the first ten pages — so viewers know the engine of the episode.

Consider moving the inciting incident into the cold open as an ironic mirror or have the event hinted at immediately with a micro-inciting incident that escalates later. For example, open on the protagonist signing up for an app that promises 'one shame-free date.' That small choice can escalate into the full inciting incident when the date goes viral.

Rewrite your first ten pages to include that early hook and upload them before our next class. Early traction makes everything after smarter.

Hook first, explain later. — Jade

task_instruction: Advise on sharpening secondary character voices with examples and model lines.
task_details: Student's secondary characters sound similar. Provide techniques to differentiate (lexicon, rhythm, physical tic) and supply two brief model lines showing how to make two side characters distinct.
personalized:
Secondary characters are currently functioning as echo chambers for your protagonist. Give them a pocket of language or a physical tic and they'll leap alive.

Make one character clipped and efficient, the other endlessly verbose and circuitous. For example, write the roommate like this: 'I'll be back in ten' and the boss like this: 'Ten is an elastic concept, Jade. In our office, it's more of a suggestion.' One is punctuation, the other is a flourish.

Try giving each supporting character a repeatable phrase or physical beat (twirling keys, a nervous laugh) and rework two pages to show the contrast. Resubmit with the changes annotated.

Distinct voices create company. Give them texture. — Jade

task_instruction: Help students clarify the episode's theme and craft a single-sentence thematic statement.
task_details: Ask students to write a single-sentence thematic statement summarizing what the episode is about emotionally, then show how that theme should be reflected in the A and B stories. Require submission of the sentence and a 100-word explanation tying both stories to the theme.
personalized:
Before you tinker with jokes, let's name the episode's heart. Write a single-sentence thematic statement that captures what the episode is about emotionally. Something clean like 'This episode asks whether fear of embarrassment is a good enough reason to avoid things that matter.'

Once you have that sentence, write a 100-word note explaining how both your A and B stories support that theme. Be explicit: which scene proves the theme and which joke undercuts it. Upload both items to the Drive by Monday.

When theme guides you, scenes stop wandering. Pick a sentence and use it like a touchstone in rewrites. — Jade

task_instruction: Prepare students for a pitch meeting with concise practice instructions and a mock pitch exercise.
task_details: Students have a simulated pitch next week. Ask them to prepare a 2-minute verbal pitch of their pilot using logline, hook, and one-paragraph character sketch. Require practicing with a timer and recording themselves, then upload the audio file.
personalized:
Mock pitch heads-up: next week you'll each give a two-minute pitch. Structure it like this: state the logline, deliver the hook (what makes the show different), and give a one-paragraph sketch of your protagonist.

Practice with a timer and record yourself. Keep it under two minutes. Put your recording in the Drive folder tonight so I can give targeted notes. Don't read; speak like you're having coffee with an exec for 120 seconds.

Polish the opening line — it's the promise. We'll workshop delivery in class. — Jade

task_instruction: Request a tag rewrite to alter the episode's tone (sweet vs. cynical).
task_details: Student wants to experiment with ending tone. Ask them to rewrite the tag twice: once with a sweet, conciliatory pay-off and once with a cynical, ironic pay-off. Provide guidance on what to change and ask for both versions submitted.
personalized:
You can change the emotional residue of an episode with one small pivot at the tag. Write two versions of your tag: one that leans sweet and resolves with warmth, and one that leans cynical and ends on an ironic twist.

For the sweet version, soften the last joke into a small, human gesture — a hand on a shoulder, a returned sweater. For the cynical version, tighten the punchline so it undercuts the protagonist's growth.

Upload both tag versions titled 'Tag_Sweet' and 'Tag_Cynic' by Sunday evening. We'll read both and discuss which better serves your season arc.

Tone change is a lever. Pull it intentionally. — Jade

task_instruction: Give an exercise to arrange beats for a 22-minute episode using index cards to pace jokes and emotional moments.
task_details: Ask students to photograph a staged index-card layout for a 22-minute episode divided into cold open, Act One, Act Two, Act Three, and tag. Cards should include beat description and approximate page targets. Require upload and a brief note explaining pacing choices.
personalized:
Pacing exercise: pretend you're building a 22-minute episode on a whiteboard. Lay out index cards for the cold open, Act One (pages 1–8), Act Two (9–16), Act Three (17–28), and tag. On each card write the beat, the emotional goal, and an approximate page target.

Take a photo of your spread and upload it along with a 150-word note explaining why you placed big jokes and emotional reveals where you did. Pay attention to where you want a laugh riot versus where you want quiet.

This will make your episode feel intentional on a runtime scale. Submit by next Wednesday. — Jade

task_instruction: Send a formatting and proofreading checklist for professional spec submission.
task_details: Provide a short checklist for spec script polish: font, margins, scene headings, slugline consistency, parentheticals, scene descriptions, page count, and proofread for typos. Ask students to confirm they've run these checks and resubmit a clean PDF.
personalized:
Final polish checklist for specs: use 12-point Courier, standard margins, consistent scene headings, slugline clarity, minimal parentheticals, scene descriptions that are lean and visual, and keep the script within the expected page count for your format. Proofread for typos and read dialogue aloud to catch rhythm issues.

Run your file through a script formatter if you haven't. Export a clean PDF and upload it with '_SpecFinal' in the filename. Reply to this email to confirm you've completed the checklist and when I should expect the file.

Presentation matters as much as jokes. Make it easy to read. — Jade

task_instruction: Teach peer-notes etiquette and how to give constructive feedback in a writers' room.
task_details: Provide guidance on delivering notes: be specific, balance praise with actionable critiques, avoid 'I don't like' without rationale, suggest alternatives, and model a short constructive note example. Encourage empathy and brevity.
personalized:
Quick guide to giving notes in our room: be specific, be kind, and be useful. Don't say 'I don't like this'; try 'This beats lands unclear because the motivation isn't stated. Try clarifying why the character chooses X.' Balance critique with what worked (praise the bit that did) and offer a concrete suggestion to fix it.

Avoid global statements without examples. If something feels off, point to a line or a moment and say why. Offer a short alternative if you can: 'Try this line instead: 'I didn't sign up for weird.' That helps rewrite time.

Example: 'Love the opening image. The A-story needs clearer stakes by page eight — maybe add a ticking deadline. Also trim the echoing jokes at pages three through five.' Short, actionable, and not mean.

Remember: we're building each other's work up, not tearing it down. Yes-and. — Jade

Dear Festival Programming Team,

I am submitting my single-camera comedy pilot, "Family Table," for consideration in your episodic competition. Attached: one-pager, pilot script, and sizzle reel. Runtime: approximately 22 minutes. Format: single-camera comedy pilot.

"Family Table" follows a Korean-American family in Los Angeles negotiating modern dating, eldercare, and unexpected career pivots. The pilot balances relationship-driven beats with sharp ensemble comedy and would fit your episodic slate that highlights diverse voices in half-hour storytelling.

Please confirm receipt of these materials and let me know your selection timeline or if you require any additional assets. I am happy to provide cast bios, a series bible, or a private screener link on request.

Thank you for your consideration.

Best regards,
Jade Kim
Writer / Story Editor
Los Angeles

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

task_instruction: Ask a former professor for a 30-minute career-advice call about staffing and a possible intro to a showrunner.

personalized:
Subject: Quick career chat and one small intro? 

Hi Professor Lee,

Hope you’re well — still think about your "character economy" lecture when I’m redrafting beats. I’m in LA now, freelancing as a staff writer/story editor on comedy pilots, and I could use a quick reality check about staffing strategies (how to pitch yourself into a room, realistic timelines, that sort of thing). Would you have 30 minutes next week for a quick call? I’m free Monday or Thursday after 2pm PT, but I can flex to fit your schedule.

Also, a small ask only if it’s not a burden: would you mind an intro to Samir Patel (showrunner, Night Shift)? He and I share a similar sensibility and I’d love to ask one question about how his rooms structure A- and B-stories. Totally fine if now’s not the right time or you don’t have his contact handy.

Appreciate any time you can spare — and thank you again for teaching me to sketch character arcs on index cards. 

Warmly,
Jade Kim (she/her)
TV writer — USC / Tisch

personalized:
Subject: Quick logline note? (20 minutes max) 

Hi Professor Chen,

I hope you’re great. I’m polishing a logline for a half-hour sitcom pilot and would value one quick read from you. Here it is: A deeply practical Korean-American woman opens a failing banchan shop in Koreatown and reluctantly becomes the neighborhood's accidental relationship counselor while trying to keep her family’s secret recipe alive.

persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

I’ll also send a reading list and a one-page assignment packet you can use. If you want local mentors to run hands-on sessions, I can introduce you to two community writers who do terrific youth workshops. Sorry I can't be there live — would love to help in a way that still serves your program. — Jade

contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Polite refusals and alternative offers. Examples: "I can't commit this semester — my rewrite schedule is full." "Happy to recommend a colleague." "Can we revisit next quarter?" Distinct features include a clear 'no' framed with reasons, and next-step suggestions or referrals.

task_instruction: Decline a local nonprofit's request for a workshop due to tight turnaround on a freelance assignment; offer to provide materials and a short webinar later in the month.
task_details: Recipient: Program manager at a nonprofit arts org asking Jade to run a workshop in two weeks. Reason for decline: tight turnaround on a freelance assignment prevents taking on new in-person workshops. Alternative: provide workshop materials (slides, exercises) and host a 60-minute webinar later that month. Tone should be supportive and community-minded.
personalized: Hi Marisol — thank you for the invitation to run a workshop in two weeks. I can't take it on with that turnaround — I'm finishing a freelance assignment and my schedule won't allow an in-person commitment. I can share the full workshop materials (slides, exercises, handouts) and host a 60-minute webinar later in the month to walk your participants through the exercises. If that timing works, I'll get the materials to you this week. — Jade

persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?"
