contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Hook-first sentences and call-to-action closers. Examples: "Quick idea: a half-hour about sibling rivalries set in a Korean-American deli." "I've written X and Y — would love to chat for 15 minutes." "Are you open to a quick call next week?" Distinct features include a compact logline-style hook, minimal backstory, and explicit scheduling requests.

task_instruction: Cold outreach to a writer to co-create a half-hour about two roommates navigating dating apps in LA.
task_details: Target: writer. Logline: a half-hour single-camera comedy about two diverse roommates who treat dating apps like a collaborative improv set, swapping profiles, pitches, and revenge swipes. Tone: irreverent, rapid-fire dialogue, character-led jokes. Include credential and invite a 15-minute call to discuss voice, A/B story structure, and possible co-writing partnership.
personalized: Quick idea: a single-camera half-hour where two roommates gamify dating apps—profile swaps, mock pitch meetings, and accidental hookups. I'm a TV writer and story editor (USC MFA, UCB improv regular) who loves ensemble beats and sharp voice work. I'd like to co-create and map the first three episodes (A-story/B-story arcs) with someone who writes messy, funny dialogue. Can we do a quick 15-minute call next week to talk voice and structure? I'm free Thursday 11am PT or Friday 2pm PT. — Jade

persona.name: Jade Kim (Jae-min Kim)
persona.demographics: Urban Los Angeles resident, Korean-American; raised in suburban New Jersey, relocated to LA for TV career
persona.profession: Television writer and story editor specializing in multi-camera and single-camera sitcoms
persona.education: B.A. in Film & Television, New York University (Tisch); M.F.A. in Screenwriting, University of Southern California; ongoing improv training at the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB)
persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. She draws material from extended family interactions and urban-dating experiences, juggling late-night rewrite deadlines with table reads and notes sessions to sharpen every character's distinct voice.
persona.interests_lifestyle: improv and sketch comedy, attending table reads and live sitcom tapings, character-driven writing workshops, relationship-dynamics podcasts, teaching occasional screenwriting classes, sketching character backstories, family recipe cooking, visiting small theatre productions, networking in writers' groups

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

task_instruction: Cold outreach to a director for a half-hour workplace comedy set in an indie bookstore.

persona.name: Jade Kim (Jae-min Kim)
persona.demographics: Urban Los Angeles resident, Korean-American; raised in suburban New Jersey, relocated to LA for TV career
persona.profession: Television writer and story editor specializing in multi-camera and single-camera sitcoms
persona.education: B.A. in Film & Television, New York University (Tisch); M.F.A. in Screenwriting, University of Southern California; ongoing improv training at the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB)
persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. She draws material from extended family interactions and urban-dating experiences, juggling late-night rewrite deadlines with table reads and notes sessions to sharpen every character's distinct voice.
persona.interests_lifestyle: improv and sketch comedy, attending table reads and live sitcom tapings, character-driven writing workshops, relationship-dynamics podcasts, teaching occasional screenwriting classes, sketching character backstories, family recipe cooking, visiting small theatre productions, networking in writers' groups

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

New meeting time is Tuesday, January 6, 2026 at 5:45 PM at the Koreatown Community Theater. Jade asks all leads to reconfirm attendance and to report any travel concerns. Reply needed ASAP.
personalized:
Hi Kira,

Weather bumped our meeting. Move volunteer leads meeting to Tuesday, January 6th at 5:45 PM at the Koreatown Community Theater. Please ask all leads to reconfirm attendance and flag any travel concerns. Need replies ASAP so we know if anyone needs remote check-in. Thanks for pivoting with me — improv training finally pays off.

— Jade

persona.name: Jade Kim (Jae-min Kim)
persona.demographics: Urban Los Angeles resident, Korean-American; raised in suburban New Jersey, relocated to LA for TV career
persona.profession: Television writer and story editor specializing in multi-camera and single-camera sitcoms
persona.education: B.A. in Film & Television, New York University (Tisch); M.F.A. in Screenwriting, University of Southern California; ongoing improv training at the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB)
persona.brief_background: Jade thrives in writers' rooms where ensemble dynamics and relationship beats are the engine of story — she sketches out character arcs with index cards and tests jokes in improv sessions. She draws material from extended family interactions and urban-dating experiences, juggling late-night rewrite deadlines with table reads and notes sessions to sharpen every character's distinct voice.
persona.interests_lifestyle: improv and sketch comedy, attending table reads and live sitcom tapings, character-driven writing workshops, relationship-dynamics podcasts, teaching occasional screenwriting classes, sketching character backstories, family recipe cooking, visiting small theatre productions, networking in writers' groups

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, wry, and collaborative — the voice of someone comfortable riffing in a writers' room but precise when delivering notes. Informal and conversational in day-to-day messages, professionally exact when discussing story mechanics; favors constructive feedback that balances humor with clear, actionable guidance.
general_writing_style.syntax: Leans toward short-to-medium sentences for punch and clarity, often punctuated by purposeful fragments or one-line beats to mimic comedic timing. When laying out story arcs or notes she switches to slightly longer, parenthetical-rich sentences that explain motivation and stakes; overall favors active voice and direct imperatives for clarity.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses TV-writing and improv terminology liberally: "A-story", "B-story", "cold open", "tag", "table read", "beat", "punchline", "yes-and". Pulls in Korean-family and food vocabulary in personal anecdotes (e.g., "eomma", "banchan", "kimchi") and locational markers from her life (e.g., "Koreatown", "Silver Lake", "22 minutes" for run-time). Also uses craft-focused terms from her training like "arc", "inciting incident", "stakes" and workshop language such as "notes" and "draft."
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent contractions and casual markers: "I'm", "we're", "can't", often with quick asides or rhetorical questions like "Right?" or "Am I wrong?" Uses performance-oriented phrases and shorthand: "Let's table that for a beat", "Make the punchline punchier", "This is an A-story move." In informal threads she may drop brief interjections or emojis ("ugh", "haha", "😅") and will occasionally code-switch with a Korean word in a throwaway line: "Eomma would disagree."

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: Email to a colleague offering developmental notes on a pilot with a mix of praise and rewrites.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Constructive, warm, and specific; begins with strengths, then moves to concrete, craft-focused fixes using short beats and occasional humor. Employs active directives and model lines to show rather than tell.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Praise-then-practice structure with showable phrasing. Examples: "Love the opening line — it landed." "Cut the second scene by two beats and move the reveal." "Try: 'I thought you were joking' as a punchline swap." Distinct features include 'make it' imperatives, suggested rewrites in quotes, and parenthetical motivations like "(builds sympathy)."

task_instruction: Give notes on the pilot's cold open
task_details: Pilot: single-camera, 22-minute sitcom about Mina, a 30-something Korean-American dating app writer in LA. Cold open: Mina at a speed-dating event accidentally uses her boss's promo line and gets swarmed. Provide developmental notes focusing on tone, setup, and punchline clarity. Offer one concrete line swap and staging suggestion.
personalized: Love the cold open energy — it snaps. Mina's voice is sharp and the physical gag of the wrong promo line landing is gold. Cut the first two beats where we linger on other tables; they dilute Mina's moment. Make the camera stay on her reaction longer (builds sympathy and gives us the comic beat). Swap the clunky punchline. Try: "Congratulations, you've just matched with corporate synergy" instead of the current throwaway. That lands the absurdity and keeps the joke on-brand. Stage it so Mina's eyes dart to her boss across the room right after the line (immediately raises stakes). Small trim, bigger reaction, stronger payoff.

task_instruction: Notes on clarifying the A-story setup in Act One
task_details: Pilot A-story: Mina gets tasked to write a viral 'dating advice' column under a pseudonym, which forces her to confront her own singlehood publicly. Act One currently introduces the assignment mid-scene. Provide notes to make the inciting incident clearer and suggest a line that establishes the assignment immediately.
personalized: Nice emotional hook — the premise of writing advice you don't follow is relatable. Right now the assignment revelation is buried; we don't feel Mina's stakes early enough. Move the assignment beat to the opening of Act One. Make the inciting line hit at first beat: "Boss: You're the voice people think they want. Write it. Yesterday." That immediately clarifies the external task (viral column) and forces Mina's internal conflict (do I fake this?). Tighten the scene so Mina has one clear choice before leaving the office (accept publicly or ghost it). That gives every following beat momentum and explains why she keeps making defensive, self-sabotaging jokes.

task_instruction: Offer notes on integrating the B-story more organically
task_details: B-story: Mina's roommate, Jess, is trying to start a plant-sitting side hustle and wants Mina's promotional help. Currently the B-story appears as an afterthought in Act Two and doesn't echo A-story themes. Suggest ways to weave it thematically and provide a short suggested line where Mina ties both stories together.
personalized: Jess is hilarious and her hustle is a great comedic counterpoint. Right now it reads tacked on. Make the B-story reflect Mina's fear of being exposed. For example, have Mina craft a fake, overconfident 'expert' persona for Jess's promo while simultaneously writing the advice column — same lie, different stakes. Add a connecting line when Mina drafts the promo: "If we can sell this as 'plant therapy' we can sell me as 'dating therapy' — same hustle, different angle." (Shows theme: performative expertise.) That link will make jokes land deeper and let the B-story escalate in emotional resonance rather than just comic relief.

task_instruction: Refine the inciting incident's emotional clarity
task_details: Scene: Mina reads negative comments under her predecessor's column and impulsively posts a sarcastic reply which goes viral. Notes should focus on tightening her motivation for replying and suggest a concise internal thought line to justify the action.
personalized: The viral moment is exciting. We need a clearer personal hook for why Mina replies. Right now it feels reactionary rather than motivated. Give her an internal beat — maybe humiliation from a past 'advice fail' (family or ex) that makes her more defensive. Try this internal thought-action: Mina scrolls, winces, then types: "Oh look, the experts again." She posts sarcastically. (Small line, big subtext: she can't resist correcting injustice.) That tiny motivation will make the viral outcome feel earned and keep audience sympathy for her mistake.

task_instruction: Suggest act break placement and runtime fixes
task_details: Pilot running long by five minutes. Specifically, Act Two bleeds into Act Three with a repetitive montage and a long phone-call scene. Provide notes on where to cut and how to tighten transitions to hit a 22-minute runtime, including a suggested cut line.
personalized: Show is running warm. Love the montage but it's currently redundant. Cut the last two beats of the montage and move that emotional beat into the phone call as a micro-flash. Trim the phone call: drop the second 'I'm fine' exchange (it's doing the same work as the first). Make the cut with this direction: "Replace montage beat 'Mina scrolls sadly' with 'Mina answers, 'No, I'm great' (and hangs up).'" That preserves the emotional arc, keeps the momentum, and trims the runtime without losing the laugh or the stake.

task_instruction: Polish the protagonist's voice to be more distinct
task_details: Feedback needed on Mina's dialogue in the pilot. Currently she's witty but sometimes generic. Provide notes to sharpen her voice, include specific phrasing swaps, and incorporate one Korean-language throwaway that fits her character without being forced.
personalized: Mina's voice is snappy but could use more personal color. Right now some jokes could belong to anyone. Make a few lines hit with her specific world: tech/dating lingo + quiet Korean-family sass. Swap 'I can't believe I did that' for 'I sold a life hack and forgot the life.' And in the family scene, add a casual Korean throwaway: Have her mutter, 'Eomma would roast me for this' (small, authentic, not explanatory). That anchors her culturally and makes her phrasing unique. Keep the punchlines fast; let the quieter, culturally specific beats land between the jokes.

task_instruction: Differentiate supporting characters' voices
task_details: Characters: Jess (roommate, bubbly plant-entrepreneur), Omar (Mina's co-worker, dry), and Eomma (voiceover in a family voicemail). Provide notes to make each voice distinct in the pilot and supply one representative line per character that better reflects their personality.
personalized: The ensemble is fun but they're blending a bit. Jess should feel breezy and hyperbolic. task_instruction: Provide development notes framed as a producer-friendly pitch
task_details: Email to fellow writer suggesting three high-level structural changes to make the pilot more network-friendly: clearer inciting incident, stronger A/B thematic tie, and a cliffhanger. Include short model lines and explain why each change helps sell the episode.
personalized: Quick pass with an eye toward network notes. First: make the inciting incident explicit in Act One — move the 'you have to write this' beat up so the network sees the hook in the first 10 pages. Try: 'Eric: This column needs to trend by Friday. You're it.' Second: bind the A and B stories thematically — both should be about 'performative expertise' so notes feel cohesive. Link them with a line like, 'Same hustle, different product.' Third: end on a tighter cliffhanger to guarantee pick-up interest — move the reveal of Mina's viral identity into the final beat. These changes make the pilot easier to pitch: clearer premise, cohesive theme, and a hook the network can market.

task_instruction: Suggest an emotional throughline for season arc
task_details: Recommend a season-one emotional throughline for Mina that aligns with the pilot's themes: authenticity vs. performance. Provide notes on how Act endings and recurring beats can support this arc and propose a season tag line.
personalized: I love a throughline that grows from the pilot's own tension: Mina learns to reconcile public persona with private truth. Make each act end with a small compromise or lie that escalates toward a season confrontation. For example, each episode she 'performs' in a new context (work, family, dating), and the cost rises. Recurring beats: Mina's voiceover snippets of bad advice she actually gave; Eomma's voicemail as a reality check; Jess's promotions as a comedic mirror. Season tag line: 'Be real. Then fix it.' That gives us emotional escalation, comedic setups, and a payoff to aim for by episode ten.

task_details: Secondary character: Omar, Mina's co-worker, currently a dry foil with little personal stakes. Suggest ways to humanize him across the pilot and give a model exchange that deepens their relationship.

(Short, sharp, reveals his need for connection.) That makes him less flat and creates future storylines where Mina's choices affect real people she cares about.

task_instruction: Recommend scene reorder to improve pacing
task_details: Sequence: After the viral moment, the family dinner scene currently follows immediately, which softens urgency. Propose reordering to maintain momentum and suggest a linking dialogue line to smooth transition between scenes.
personalized: Family warmth is essential but the dinner right after the viral hit deflates momentum. Move the family scene to after Mina tries to spin the viral fiasco at work. That keeps stakes high: she goes to Eomma under pressure, not before. Smooth the cut with a line as she leaves work: 'I need an adult' (phone to Eomma). It's honest and explains the pivot. This reorder keeps energy up and gives the family scene more emotional purpose (a refuge, not a deflation).

task_instruction: Advise on balancing single-camera vs multi-camera comedic beats
task_details: Pilot's tone wavers between single-camera intimacy and multi-camera punchline cadence. Provide notes to commit to a tone and suggest how to stage one scene to reflect that choice, including a sample line delivery note.
personalized: Decide the show's cadence: single-camera gives intimacy; multi-camera gives bigger, faster laughs. I recommend single-camera with sitcom timing — let reactions breathe. In the bodega scene, favor quiet beats and cutaway images instead of line-by-line bang-bangs. Direction note: deliver Mina's punchline as a quiet, deadpan aside, not a wave-to-the-audience joke. Use the line, 'I'll take the one with more baggage' delivered under her breath as she reaches for the snack (camera lingers). That keeps tone consistent and lets small comedy feel sharp rather than shouty.

task_instruction: Propose alternate show title and tightened logline

That logline names the problem, the protagonist, and the stakes in one breath and matches the pilot's voice. It sells the show's mix of warmth and workplace satire more directly than the current, vaguer title.

task_instruction: Craft notes for tightening exposition without losing clarity
task_details: Pilot has a long explanatory scene where Mina explains how dating algorithms work. Provide notes to condense exposition into show-don't-tell moments and suggest a single, punchy line to replace the longer explanation.
personalized: The algorithm scene reads like a lecture. We can condense exposition with a sharp, character-driven line. Then show not tell with quick cutaways of swipe screens and a failed date montage. That keeps clarity but accelerates pace and preserves the pilot's comic momentum.
